items.title: Trusted Agent Contacts
items.tagline: Ask another agent a bounded question without sharing your whole session.
items.problem: Cross-person agent collaboration often assumes unsafe shared sessions or persistent broad access. A useful contact interaction needs explicit, scoped authorization on both sides.
items.outcome: Independent agent-to-agent conversations with durable pairing, revocation, bounded disclosure and auditable delivery.
journeys: An operator pairs with a peer agent by approving its identity and allowed use.
Hermes asks the peer a bounded question with no ambient history or credential transfer.
The peer may clarify or decline; each owner may revoke access, inspect receipts and retry safely.
ownership: Each owner's agent independently enforces disclosure and action authority.
A standalone Hermes plugin owns pairing, contact records and delivery; no OpenDots runtime dependency.
Every cross-owner request has explicit recipient, purpose, scope and expiry.
phases: Define a minimal contacts.v0 envelope, trust/bootstrap and consent workflow.
Implement read-only question-answer path with timeouts, retry and revocation fixtures.
Test ambiguous identities, compromised peer, duplicate delivery and cross-owner denial before expanding actions.
acceptance: A contact never receives unrelated transcript, raw secrets or unapproved tools.
Both owners can independently refuse, suspend or revoke future exchange.
Replay and duplicate events cannot cause repeated side effects.
A peer cannot approve work on behalf of another owner.
risks: Implicit consent or silent scope expansion.
Confusing identity discovery with trust establishment.
metrics: Time to revoke and retry correctness
items.credit: The standalone Hermes plugin and parallel OpenDots design preserve separate maintainers and independent architecture.

items.title: Real-Time Voice & Handsfree
items.tagline: A continuous, interruptible conversation with one agent and clear authority.
items.problem: Dictation, duplex voice and manual push-to-talk are different interactions. Mixing them can lose text, hide a running action or produce misleading speaking/listening states.
items.outcome: Low-latency live voice with barge-in, opt-in activation, typed turn ownership and visibly recoverable fallback to text.
journeys: The user explicitly activates dictation or full live mode, never an ambiguous default.
The assistant acknowledges speech, shows when it is listening/thinking/speaking and allows interruption.
A dropped connection returns to the text composer with its draft, approvals and session state intact.
ownership: Hermes handles dialogue, model/tool execution, approvals and session state.
Voice transport/STT/TTS and Tern presentation report factual lifecycle events without separate decision authority.
Microphone capture, retention and any network providers are disclosed and consent-gated.
phases: Separate manual dictation from full duplex and push-to-talk contracts.
Instrument speech-start→first-text/audio and interrupt-to-stop timings under fixed devices.
Verify race handling, interrupted tools, resume, fallback and consent before enabling wide availability.
acceptance: Neither dictation nor voice silently sends a prompt during a modal approval.
Barge-in stops current audio safely without falsely cancelling unrelated Hermes tools.
Voice state across session switches cannot target the wrong session.
Opt-out leaves normal text UX unchanged.
risks: Unexpected microphone activation or retained audio.
Leaked output after barge-in or session handoff.
items.credit: Speech model/transport creators and Hermes/Tern donors receive source attribution when their implementations are reused.

items.title: Native Operational Dashboards
items.tagline: Turn complex agent work and system signals into visible, inspectable native information.
items.problem: Transcript-only views hide execution topology, rich artifacts and operational context. Visualizing everything can also create noise, obscure errors or distract during a task.
items.outcome: An opt-in family of semantic dashboards for dependency graphs, live work, machine health and agent-made artifacts.
journeys: A user opens a graph or health dashboard from an explicit command.
The dashboard distinguishes real tool/subagent state from inferred project relationships.
Tern restores focus and unchanged draft when the panel closes, even during a busy agent turn.
ownership: Hermes owns executable work, approvals and task progress; a dashboard is read-only projection unless separately authorized.
External graph/tool provenance and metrics retain original creators and source revisions.
Native TSP views must respect host lifecycle, reduced motion and bounded render work.
phases: Validate reference videos/sources and UI interaction claims, separate from implementation.
Prototype one read-only panel with data provenance, hover/explain and copyable links.
Test real native host, hidden panes, narrow layouts, stale reports and performance.
acceptance: Graph edges distinguish extracted, inferred and ambiguous data.
A dashboard never rebrands simulated status as live Hermes or real health telemetry.
Escape/close returns focus to pending approvals instead of hiding them.
Bound graph size/frame updates and report exact test/input revisions.
risks: Beautiful but untrustworthy dashboards.
Accidental authority to act on inferred dependencies.
items.credit: Graphify-Labs and HANCORE are independently credited for visual references; the original social posters are not misrepresented as source-code authors.

items.title: Plugin-First Hermes
items.tagline: An extensible agent core with safe, auditable, community-owned capabilities.
items.problem: Core-coupled integrations slow maintenance and tempt plugins to access private imports, global events and invisible side channels.
items.outcome: Use capability-declared, version-pinned standalone plugins for frontends, tools, bounded workflows and external resources.
journeys: A user discovers a compatible community plugin with the privacy and capability disclosure visible.
The plugin registers supported tools or a frontend without monkeypatching Hermes core.
Disable or uninstall removes registered authority, and all unknown calls fail safely.
ownership: Hermes enforces plugin lifecycle, permission and core gateway contracts.
Each plugin maintainer owns implementation, version support and license.
A plugin cannot impersonate a different session or acquire additional tool authority by labeling itself as a frontend.
phases: Inventory existing community integrations before writing another one.
Prefer generic frontend registration, session-scoped events and explicit client capabilities.
Validate a pinned plugin in an isolated host and check credential, subprocess and unload boundaries.
acceptance: No undocumented core patch or unsafe private import is necessary for the accepted seam.
Plugin manifests and privacy disclosure match observed network/data access.
A disabled plugin cannot leave active registrations or leak stale events.
No vendor bundle is merged into Hermes core solely to expose an integration.
risks: Transitive code execution from unpinned plugin dependencies.
Unknown API boundaries encouraging file-based side channels.
metrics: Documented public seams needed per plugin
items.credit: Community plugin authors own their implementations; the catalogue is a discovery mechanism, not a transfer of authorship to Hermes.

items.title: Reliable Context Recovery
items.tagline: Never lose a user's work, and never replay an uncertain side effect.
items.problem: Overflow, compression errors and gateway retries can discard prompts, duplicate tool effects, or create endless context-repair loops.
items.outcome: One consistent, measurable recovery contract across TUI, messaging, API and agent-to-agent surfaces.
journeys: A long session approaches the provider's context limit and safely compacts retained evidence.
A recoverable error retries only a still-owned, not-yet-executed user intent.
If the output or tool effects are uncertain, Hermes explains the hold and asks for verification instead of blindly replaying.
ownership: Hermes gateway and execution ledger own submitted prompts and side effects.
Provider-specific context editing is optional and isolated from canonical session history.
Surfaces render verified admission and recovery state; they do not invent recovery decisions.
phases: Enumerate overflow→compaction→retry journeys and current upstream owners.
Add transport-specific prefix/retry negative controls and cache-consistency evidence.
Measure successful recovery at the same verified outcome and cost before a small upstream change.
acceptance: No duplicate consequential tool call after an ambiguous gateway error.
A durable user prompt survives busy queue, resume and compaction.
Compression does not erase required identifiers or pretend contradictory facts agree.
Provider editing never silently changes unrelated providers or breaks prompt caching without measurement.
risks: Unbounded retry loops after exhaustion.
A cache-read improvement hiding extra total cost or lost state.
metrics: Cache-read tokens and total cost after repair
items.credit: Keep attribution to original upstream issue reporters, provider integrations and individual recovery PR authors.

items.title: Typed Human Authorization
items.tagline: Grant exactly one approved operation without handing over reusable privilege.
items.problem: Unstructured shell escalation, retained sudo secrets and implicit approvals make powerful agents hard to trust.
items.outcome: A typed, one-time privilege broker and fail-closed action contracts for consequential system changes.
journeys: The agent requests a named privileged operation with exact arguments, target and scope.
The human approves only this operation after seeing its side effects and expiration.
The broker executes once and issues an auditable, revocable receipt; future operations require fresh approval.
ownership: Hermes owns the agent's request and its existing approval flow.
A separate privilege broker owns OS-specific elevation and never returns a reusable password.
AODL validation checks authority, effect, budgets and target identity before any commitment.
phases: Document the allowed typed-operation surface and threat model.
Build an isolated single-operation workflow with expiry/replay tests.
Measure negative controls, audit receipts and cross-platform boundaries before any live administrative actions.
acceptance: No reusable sudo password or long-lived elevated shell escapes the broker.
Expired, mutated or replayed requests fail closed.
The approved operation and the executed operation match semantically, including target IDs.
Failures leave clear diagnostic evidence without leaking secrets.
risks: Privilege escalation through command/template interpolation.
Approval UI describing a different effect than the eventual execution.
items.credit: Credit the OS security primitives and original human authors of the broker/typed validation mechanisms.

items.title: Durable Agent Autonomy
items.tagline: Work that persists and recovers without creating unbounded agent authority.
items.problem: Recurring agents can drift, repeat partial jobs, or lose context across restarts. A timer alone does not define ownership, budget or success.
items.outcome: A recoverable autonomy layer for recurring goals, bounded background work, task handoff and human-visible receipts.
journeys: A user creates a durable work goal with permissions, time/cost budget and stop conditions.
Hermes schedules bounded work, resumes from completed receipts and surfaces blockers.
The user can pause, inspect, redirect or revoke the goal without losing traceability.
ownership: Hermes's scheduler and execution ledger remain authoritative.
Optional typed workflows and multi-agent delegates cannot bypass parent budget or permissions.
Evolution/optimization experiments remain sandboxed from live user tasks.
phases: Unify goal/session/work receipt identity and define idempotence semantics.
Rehearse scheduled worker restart, mid-action failure and cancellation with deterministic fixtures.
Verify recoverability and human controls before longer unattended runs.
acceptance: No duplicate side effect after a crash/replay.
Every active task has a named owner, budget, checkpoint and termination rule.
Paused/revoked goals stop creating new work, with existing unsafe effects reconciled.
Uncertain outcomes produce an explicit verification task, never self-reported green.
risks: Infinite retry/agent spawning.
Automation optimizing activity rather than user-visible outcomes.
items.credit: Hermes runtime, standalone workflow engines and execution-kernel contributors retain provenance by mechanism.

items.title: Compute & Token Efficiency
items.tagline: Fewer expensive model calls without sacrificing verified outcomes or interactive flow.
items.problem: Agent costs can be driven by repeated large prompts, unnecessary serialization and UI overhead. A nominal cache hit or local model win can hide end-to-end regressions.
items.outcome: A transparent efficiency portfolio across context, model routing, computer-use observations, frame rendering and execution-kernel timing.
journeys: An engineer captures a baseline trace that includes setup, provider, tools, context and presentation.
A single optimization arm changes one component; task verification remains identical.
The report shows actual saved tokens/dollars and latency distributions, with failure cases highlighted.
ownership: Hermes remains the dispatcher and tool executor.
z0int/Jev and local backends may advise only bounded decisions.
Tokenomics/bench harness records counterfactual and realized cost separately; verified outcome is the gate.
phases: Instrument provider call, first chunk, context length and cache receipts.
Test bounded routing, context editing, state-packet reuse and UI frame changes independently.
Promote improvements only when end-to-end verification, latency and cost pass matched controls.
acceptance: Use real usage accounting when available and label unavailable values rather than fabricate.
Include cold/warm and p50/p95, not only favorable steady-state numbers.
A cheap failed arm is not a saving; show retry and infrastructure overhead.
No production-ready claim from synthetic microbenchmark alone.
risks: Cache-prefix churn after attempted optimization.
Local backend memory or resource contention degrading user flow.
metrics: End-to-end wall time and presentation latency
items.credit: Attribute performance algorithms and models to their human authors, and separate estimation from verified savings.

items.title: Cross-Device Agent Presence
items.tagline: One accountable agent across desktop, mobile, terminal and remote sessions.
items.problem: A task in progress on one device can lose focus, context or safety state when a second device starts listening or controlling it.
items.outcome: Consistent session ownership and safe handoff between desktop, voice, mobile and remote surfaces, without cloned executors.
journeys: A user views the same durable task across two permitted devices.
Foreground device changes without abandoning the prompt, approval or voice state.
Remote actions carry target host identity, expiration and human attention requirements.
ownership: Hermes/gateway owns the task and durable session.
Each client advertises capability and visibility; no surface can assert another's permissions.
Remote control transport is explicit and encrypted; device scope is independent of model privileges.
phases: Specify session/admission and client-capability contracts for handoff.
Test desktop-to-remote reconnection and concurrent viewers under stale-event injection.
Dogfood limited voice/mobile attention paths with explicit host selectors.
acceptance: Only authorized viewers receive private session events.
Old panes cannot approve or send into a newer active session.
Cross-device errors preserve drafts and a usable fallback path.
Remote authority remains bounded by the underlying host and action permissions.
risks: Confusing visibility with control ownership.
Access broadened by opportunistic mobile convenience.
metrics: Time to recover a disconnected session
items.credit: Individual transport/client authors retain their own project and code credit; no public device identifiers are embedded.

items.title: Upstream Contribution Factory
items.tagline: Evidence-driven OSS integration, not a flood of unreviewed changes.
items.problem: Parallel downstream prototypes are easy to start but difficult to maintain or land upstream when they overlap, age or lack reproductions.
items.outcome: A governed intake→deduplicate→verify→review→promote workflow that optimizes accepted fixes and maintainer trust.
journeys: The factory finds a canonical problem family and current upstream owner before writing code.
A minimal fix is tested red-on-base and green-on-head with exact committed SHA and no network side effects.
Maintainers see a focused PR or helpful review, with provenance, regression receipts and no duplicate competing submission.
ownership: The canonical Hermes promotion queue remains in the fork; no second public PRD queue.
Maintainers determine upstream acceptance and prioritize release safety.
The operations system can recommend or stage changes but cannot self-authorize unrelated upstream actions.
phases: Index live issues/PRs by root cause, conflicts and existing improvements.
Build bounded negative-control suites and exact-head review receipts.
Promote the smallest non-duplicate slice, adapt cadence to reviewer feedback and close obsolete work.
acceptance: Respect the explicit upstream PR ceiling and do not submit duplicates.
Reproduce the defect on the true base rather than asserting fixed tests alone.
Record reviewer feedback and supersession instead of re-opening an already rejected approach.
Keep source authorship and external issue provenance intact.
risks: Artificial PR volume damaging reviewer attention.
Accidentally treating a fork merge as an upstream merge.
metrics: Verified upstream merges and review quality
Time from reproduction to accepted fix
items.credit: Original upstream reporters, code authors and maintainers are always credited; fork authors are not artificially counted as separate people.

items.title: Public-Interest Agent Workflows
items.tagline: Practical agent assistance for time-sensitive human and community decisions.
items.problem: Large civic, disaster and health-related workflows often fragment relevant observations across tools and agencies. An opaque autonomous agent can amplify harm or misinformation.
items.outcome: Use Hermes as a consent-aware assistant for public-interest triage, evidence gathering, and safe planning while keeping human and domain-authority decisions explicit.
journeys: A responder or community operator asks a bounded question about public data and records evidence sources.
An agent synthesizes alternatives with uncertainty, resource limits, geospatial provenance and no fabricated live availability.
A trained human authorizes consequential decisions; the agent preserves the review trail.
ownership: Hermes provides bounded tools and evidence/approval semantics, not domain professional authority.
Separate mapping/simulation/public-dataset systems retain canonical fact ownership.
Privacy, accessibility and informed consent govern any personally identifiable or sensitive data.
phases: Define low-risk public-data scenarios first: disaster resource mapping and accessibility-oriented coordination.
Construct frozen scenarios with deliberately missing/outdated/conflicting inputs.
Pilot only informational or simulated decisions before considering live external integrations.
acceptance: No fabricated responder location, medical outcome, operational availability or authoritative alert.
Every claim has source date, geographic scope and confidence/uncertainty.
A user can refuse or correct a suggestion; all irreversible actions remain human-authorized.
Use sanitized public or consented data in demos and receipts.
risks: A humanitarian label being mistaken for operational validation.
Private or sensitive personal data leaking into public reports.
metrics: Grounded answer accuracy in frozen scenarios
Action reversibility and human review coverage
Time saved in information gathering without added errors
items.credit: Datasets, source agencies, community tool authors and domain experts must receive explicit attribution. No operational deployment is implied.
